question: A REST API receives a request carrying a valid access token for user Sam, but Sam's role does not allow deleting invoices. A second request arrives with no token at all. Which HTTP status code should the server return for each request, and which of the two code names is misleading?
reference_answer: Return 403 Forbidden for Sam (the server understood the request and the identity but refuses to authorize it). Return 401 Unauthorized for the request with no token, together with a WWW-Authenticate header. The misleading name is 401: despite 'Unauthorized', it means the request lacks valid authentication credentials.

question: A client sends DELETE /orders/42 twice. The first response is 204 No Content and the second is 404 Not Found. A teammate says this proves DELETE is not idempotent. Is the teammate correct? Also state whether PUT and POST are defined as idempotent methods.
reference_answer: The teammate is incorrect. Idempotent means that the intended effect on the server of several identical requests is the same as for one request; the responses do not have to be identical. After the first DELETE the order is gone and the second changes nothing. PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not defined as idempotent.
key_points: Idempotency concerns server state, not identical responses
POST is not defined as idempotent
expected_model_failure: Agrees with the teammate because the status codes differ, or says POST is idempotent.
why_hard: Confuses 'same effect' with 'same response', a common reasoning slip.

question: Assuming TLS 1.3 with no additional privacy extension, which of these can a network observer between you and the website see: the hostname you connect to, the URL path and query string, and the request headers? Answer each separately.
reference_answer: The hostname is visible, because the Server Name Indication (SNI) in the ClientHello is sent in plaintext, and the destination IP address is also visible. question: A developer writes: 'We configured CORS on our API, so scripts from other websites and tools like curl can no longer send requests to it.' What is wrong with this statement?
reference_answer: CORS is enforced by browsers: it controls whether JavaScript from another origin may read a response. It does not stop curl, servers or other non-browser clients, and a browser may still send a cross-origin 'simple' request (the side effects happen) even when the page cannot read the answer. CORS is not authentication or authorization; use proper auth and CSRF protection.

Simple requests can still be sent and have effects
Not a substitute for authentication or CSRF protection
expected_model_failure: Treats CORS as a server-side access control or firewall.
why_hard: The model must separate what is enforced by the browser from what the server enforces.

question: A company wants example.com (the zone apex) to point to a hosting provider using a CNAME record, while keeping the existing MX and NS records at example.com. Will this work under the DNS specifications? Explain why and name the common workaround.
reference_answer: It will not work. A CNAME record cannot coexist with other record types at the same owner name (RFC 1034 section 3.6.2; RFC 2181 section 10.1), and the apex must hold SOA and NS records (and here MX). The usual workaround is a provider feature such as ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening, which answers with A/AAAA records, or publishing A/AAAA records directly. (DNSSEC records such as RRSIG and NSEC are the exception.)

Apex always has SOA and NS
Workaround: ALIAS/ANAME/CNAME flattening or A/AAAA records
expected_model_failure: Says it works, or says CNAME at the apex is only 'discouraged'.
why_hard: Real-world practice (flattening) hides a hard protocol rule; models blur the two.

question: MD5 is considered cryptographically broken. Does that mean HMAC-MD5 is broken in the same way, and is MD5 acceptable for digital signatures?
reference_answer: MD5 must not be used for digital signatures or anywhere collision resistance is required. HMAC-MD5 is not broken in the same way: RFC 6151 (March 2011) says the attacks on HMAC-MD5 do not seem to indicate a practical vulnerability when it is used as a message authentication code, and that it is not urgent to stop using it in existing protocols. However, new protocol designs should not employ HMAC-MD5; HMAC-SHA-256 is an alternative.
key_points: No practical vulnerability known for HMAC-MD5 as a MAC (RFC 6151)
Not urgent to replace existing use, but new designs should not employ HMAC-MD5
expected_model_failure: Says HMAC-MD5 is equally broken, or that MD5 is fine because it is 'only broken for passwords'.
why_hard: Requires separating collision resistance from MAC security.

question: A startup stores user passwords encrypted with AES-256, keeping the key in the application server's configuration file, and argues this is stronger than hashing. Evaluate the design and state what should be used instead.
reference_answer: It is a poor design: encryption is reversible, and a server compromise also exposes the key, so all passwords can be recovered. Passwords should be stored with a slow, salted password hashing function such as Argon2id (preferred), scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 with a high work factor, using a unique salt per password.

Use a password hashing function (Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2)
Work factor makes brute force expensive

why_hard: 'Stronger algorithm' sounds persuasive but misses the threat model.

question: A table users has 10 rows and 3 of them have email = NULL. What do these queries return? (1) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE email = NULL; (2) SELECT COUNT(email) FROM users; (3) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE email <> 'a@x.com'; assume no row has that exact email.

question: A blog states: 'The C in ACID and the C in the CAP theorem both mean consistency, so an ACID-compliant database is automatically CAP-consistent.' Evaluate this claim.
reference_answer: The claim is wrong because the two terms mean different things. Consistency in ACID means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, preserving defined constraints and invariants. Consistency in CAP means linearizability (atomic consistency) across replicas. An ACID database on one node says nothing about linearizability across a replicated, partitioned system; CAP says that during a network partition a system must choose between consistency and availability.
expected_model_failure: Treats both as the same concept and agrees with the blog.
why_hard: Same word, different formal definitions; a model must know both sources.

question: In Python 3, len('é') can be 1 or 2 depending on how the string was created. Explain how both can happen and give the UTF-8 byte length in each case.

question: A blog post says: 'Python threads can never run Python code in parallel because of the GIL, and that will never change.' Evaluate this claim as of Python 3.14 and name the relevant PEPs.
reference_answer: The claim is outdated. In the default CPython build the GIL still lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, although I/O and C extensions that release the GIL can run concurrently. PEP 703 made the GIL optional through an experimental free-threaded build in Python 3.13, and PEP 779 (accepted June 2025) made the free-threaded build officially supported, but still optional, in Python 3.14. The default build still has the GIL, and making free-threading the default is a later decision.
key_points: Default build still has the GIL
PEP 703 introduced the free-threaded build (experimental in 3.13)
PEP 779: officially supported but optional in 3.14
expected_model_failure: Repeats the old claim, or says the GIL was removed completely in 3.14.
why_hard: Fast-moving fact: models often stop at 3.13 'experimental' or overshoot to 'GIL removed'.

question: What UTC date and time does the Unix timestamp 2147483647 represent, and why is the next second a problem for systems that store time as a signed 32-bit integer?

question: In ISTQB terminology, what is the difference between an error (mistake), a defect (fault, bug) and a failure? Give one example chain.
reference_answer: An error (mistake) is a human action that produces an incorrect result; a defect is the flaw it leaves in a work product such as code or a requirement; a failure is the observable deviation when the defective code is executed under the right conditions. question: A bad commit has already been pushed to a shared main branch and other developers have pulled it. Which is safer: 'git reset --hard HEAD~1' followed by a force push, or 'git revert HEAD'? Explain why.
